title: Number and Shape Patterns Grade 3: Find the Rule (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Number and Shape Patterns Grade 3 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Number and shape patterns Grade 3 made simple: find the rule, continue the sequence and fill gaps. Free 8-question quiz plus printable practice.
excerpt: By Grade 3 the pattern question changes. It is no longer 'what comes next' but 'what is the rule'. Here is how to teach children to name the rule, extend a sequence and fill the gaps — with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Show a Grade 1 child the row 2, 4, 6, 8 and they will happily say ‘10’. Show the same row to a Grade 3 child and the honest answer you want is different: ‘the rule is add 2, so the next one is 10.’ That small shift — from guessing the next term to stating the rule — is the whole point of number and shape patterns in Grade 3. Once a child can name the rule, they can jump forward, work backward, and fill a hole anywhere in the sequence, not just at the end.

I have taught this to eight- and nine-year-olds for years, and the children who struggle are almost never the ones who cannot count. They are the ones who were never asked to describe what is happening in words. So that is where we start.

Number patterns: hunt for the rule first

A number pattern is just a list of numbers made by repeating one instruction. The instruction is the rule. In Grade 3 the rules come in two flavours, and children need both.

Adding or subtracting a constant

These are the gentlest. Look at the gap between one term and the next; if it is always the same, you have found the rule. In 5, 9, 13, 17 the gap is always +4. In 40, 35, 30, 25 the rule is −5. The tip I drill hardest: write the gap between the numbers before you guess. A child who pencils in ‘+4’ between each pair almost never gets it wrong.

Multiplying or skip-counting

This is the genuinely new Grade 3 idea, and it leans on the times tables. In 3, 6, 9, 12 the rule can be said two ways — ‘add 3’ or ‘the multiples of 3’. Both are correct, and I want children to notice both. In 2, 4, 8, 16 the gap keeps changing, so ‘add something’ fails; the rule is ‘multiply by 2’ (doubling). The moment a child spots that a growing gap usually means multiplying, a whole class of patterns opens up.

Odd, even and multiples

Grade 3 is also where number patterns meet number properties. Skip-counting by 2 from 1 gives the odd numbers; from 2 gives the even numbers. Counting in 5s gives numbers ending in 0 or 5. These are patterns children can predict without adding at all, and pointing that out builds real number sense.

How to describe a rule in words

Naming the rule out loud is not a nicety — it is the skill. A good rule statement has two parts: where you start and what you repeat. ‘Start at 7, add 6 each time.’ That is enough to rebuild the entire sequence. I ask children to say it in exactly that shape every single time, because a vague ‘it goes up’ cannot fill a gap in the middle, but a precise rule can.

Continuing a sequence and filling the gaps

Once the rule is named, two jobs follow. Continuing means applying the rule forward: 6, 11, 16, __ becomes 21. Filling a gap is where the rule really earns its keep. Given 4, __, 12, 16, a child who knows the rule is +4 fills the blank with 8 without touching the numbers on either side. And working backward matters too: given __, 15, 20, 25, subtract 5 to find the missing 10. Backward is where mistakes hide, so practise it deliberately.

Shape patterns: repeating, growing and rotating

Shape patterns follow the same ‘find the rule’ logic, but the rule is about position or size instead of value.

  • Repeating patterns have a unit that repeats: circle, square, square, circle, square, square… The rule is the repeating unit. Find where it starts over and you can predict any position.
  • Growing patterns get bigger by a fixed amount: a triangle of 1 dot, then 3, then 6, then 10. These are the bridge to number patterns, because you can write the count under each shape and hunt for the rule.
  • Rotating patterns keep the same shape but turn it: an arrow pointing up, right, down, left, then up again. The rule is a quarter-turn each time.

A neat classroom move: turn a shape pattern into a number pattern by counting sides, dots or corners. Suddenly a ‘shape’ question is a number question in disguise, and children who love drawing find a way in.

A quick guide to spotting the rule

What you seeLikely ruleExample
Same gap each timeAdd a constant7, 11, 15, 19 (+4)
Getting smaller by a fixed stepSubtract a constant30, 24, 18, 12 (−6)
Gap keeps growingMultiply / double3, 6, 12, 24 (×2)
Times-table numbersMultiples / skip-count5, 10, 15, 20
Shapes repeat in blocksFind the repeating unit▲■▲■▲■

One honest caveat

Some sequences have more than one sensible rule, and that is fine. The row 2, 4 could be ‘add 2’ or ‘double’. Do not mark a child wrong for a rule that genuinely fits — ask them to give one more term to show which rule they mean. Teaching them to defend a rule is worth more than teaching them the ‘right’ answer.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly these ideas — number rules, multiples, and shape patterns at Grade 3 level. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded pattern questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Patterns Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on number rules, multiples and shape patterns. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: The gap between each number is the same: 10 − 6 = 4, 14 − 10 = 4. The rule is add 4.
The rule is add 5 (the multiples of 5), so after 20 comes 25.
The rule is add 4. So 4 + 4 = 8 fills the blank, and 8 + 4 = 12 checks out.
The gap keeps growing (2, 4, 8), so it is not adding a constant. Each number is double the one before: multiply by 2.

questions.q: Which list shows only even numbers?
questions.explanation: Skip-counting by 2 from 2 gives the even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8.
The rule is add 7 (the multiples of 7). Going back one step from 21 means 21 − 7 = 14.

questions.q: In the pattern circle, square, square, circle, square, square, what comes next?
questions.explanation: The repeating unit is circle, square, square. After the second square, the unit starts again with a circle.

questions.q: A growing dot pattern goes 1, 3, 6, 10. How many dots come next?
questions.explanation: The gaps grow by one each time: +2, +3, +4. So the next gap is +5, giving 10 + 5 = 15.

faq.q: What patterns should a Grade 3 child know?
faq.a: Number patterns made by adding or subtracting a constant, skip-counting and multiplying (doubling), plus odd, even and multiples. In shapes they should handle repeating, growing and rotating patterns, and be able to state the rule in words.

faq.q: How do I explain the difference between adding and multiplying patterns?
faq.a: Look at the gaps. If the gap between terms stays the same, the rule is add a constant. If the gap keeps growing, the rule is usually multiply — for example 3, 6, 12, 24 doubles each time.

faq.q: Why does my child struggle to fill a gap in the middle of a sequence?
faq.a: Because they are reading left to right instead of using the rule. Once a child names the rule — say, add 4 — they can fill any blank by stepping forward or backward from a known number, not just guessing the next term.

faq.q: Can a pattern have more than one correct rule?
faq.a: Sometimes, yes. The pair 2, 4 fits both add 2 and double. Ask your child to give one more term to show which rule they mean; defending a rule matters more than picking the ‘official’ one.
